To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the following properties of a network are stably computably by anonymous, finite-state devices: the number of vertices, the number of edges, whether there are cycles, whether the network is connected, and whether the degree of every vertex is bounded by a constant.

the following predicates are stably computible in any weakly connected network graph: (i) the number of nodes, (ii) the number of edges, (iii) whether the degree of every node is bounded by a fixed number d, (iv) whether the network is connected, (v) whether the network has a cycle, and (vi) whether the network contains a node of degree d.

(a) a large class of network predicates are stably computably by the devices, (b) this class of predicates can be characterized in a simple, intuitive way, and (c) the devices can detect the network degree and organize a computation that asymptotically optimizes the memory use.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: given a finite-state device with a limited amount of memory, what properties of an ad-hoc network can be stably detected by the device?
the question of what properties of a network graph can be determined by a distributed algorithm running on a network of anonymous finite-state devices.
the question of what can be stably learned by finite-state devices in a communication network.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the class of stabled computable predicates is precisely the class of predicates that are invariant with respect to the multiset of the final values of the inputs, and that are invariant with repect to permutations of these values.

in any weakly connected network of finite-state devices, the devices can detect the maximum degree of the network graph and then stably compute a large class of functions of the multiset over the final inputs.
in a network of n anonymous, finite-state sensors, any property that is computable in time polynomial in n is stably computable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the devices can detect whether the topology is a tree, and, if it is, organize a computation with asymptotically optimal memory use, but cannot distinguish a cycle from a tree, and cannot detect the presence of a cycle in a graph with a cycle.
the devices can stably compute the degree of a network, and, if it is constant, can stably compute all predicates that can be stably decided in a weakly-connected network with a single input.
we have shown that the network topology is not a bottleneck for stabilizing computations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a large class network properties can be stably detected by devices in the network, even in the absence of any centralized control.
a large class (in fact, a large fraction) of properties of network graphs are stably computably by anonymous, finite-state devices in any weakly connected network.

, despite the lack of global information about the network topology and the absence of a global clock, the devices can stably compute properties of the network that are useful for distributed coordination and control.
